hook: Demo day is easy. **Day 400** is the job — upserts, sizing, tenants, and the restore you pray you'll never need.

scenes.title: Corpora **change**. Indexes must too.
scenes.sub: Upserts, deletes, re-indexes — the write side of retrieval
scenes.narration: Your store's contents are a living dataset: documents get edited, revoked, superseded. The write operations: upsert — insert or replace by ID, the workhorse; delete — remove a vector, harder for ANN indexes than inserts, since graphs must be repaired; re-index — rebuild the whole structure after big changes or parameter updates. The engineering rules: idempotency — the same upsert twice is safe; versioning — tag vectors with source-document versions so a re-ingest can replace exactly; and change-data-capture — feed updates from your source system rather than periodic full rebuilds.

items.s: doc_id + chunk_index = deterministic ID → re-ingestion replaces, never duplicates
ANN graphs repair lazily; budget for it at scale — or tombstone + periodic compact
Source-system events drive incremental updates; full rebuilds are the fallback, not the rhythm

scenes.narration: Write-path discipline. Deterministic IDs — document ID plus chunk index — make re-runs idempotent by construction: same input, same IDs, replaced not duplicated. Deletes: HNSW handles them, but graph repair costs show up as latency jitter; at high delete volume, many teams tombstone and compact on a schedule. And architecture: wire updates as events from the source — a file changes, a row updates — rather than nightly diff-and-rebuild. Your pipeline from Stage 3 applies verbatim: streaming updates, logs, resumability. The retrieval store is only as fresh as its write path.

scenes.title: Memory math: **vectors × dimensions × overhead**
scenes.sub: Size the index, the graph, and the headroom — before purchase
scenes.narration: Sizing a vector deployment is arithmetic plus margin. Raw vectors: count times dimensions times bytes — a million 1,536-dim float32 vectors is about six gigabytes. The index multiplies: HNSW's graph links add roughly twenty to fifty percent. Then the runtime needs headroom for queries, filters, and the operating system — double the total for comfort, and that's your node. Quantization — float16 or PQ codes — can halve-to-tenth the footprint at a recall cost you've already learned to measure. Do this math in the proposal, not after the incident.

items.s: ×1.3-1.5 for HNSW links ×2 for headroom ≈ 16-18GB node — the whole estimate
float16 = half memory · PQ = ~10x smaller at measured recall cost
Corpus doubles yearly? Shard before the node fills — resharding a full store is surgery

scenes.narration: The sizing playbook. Arithmetic first — the formula fits on an index card. Quantization when memory or cost bites, gated by your golden-set recall as always. And the growth conversation: if the corpus doubles annually, plan shard boundaries now — moving a hundred-million-vector store to a new topology under load is the kind of weekend that builds character. Better: shard by tenant or by hash at a size where rebalancing is a routine operation. Capacity planning is unglamorous and absolutely the difference between sleep and pages.

scenes.title: One store, many tenants — **isolation is the product**
scenes.narration: Every serious deployment is multi-tenant, and the isolation model is an architecture decision with security weight. Option one: shared collection with a tenant filter on every query — cheapest, but the filter must NEVER be forgettable; one missing clause is a data breach. Option two: per-tenant collections or partitions — isolation by construction, more overhead, cleaner audit. Option three: separate databases or clusters per tenant — maximum assurance, maximum cost — reserved for regulated tiers. Choose per tenant class, enforce at the retrieval interface — the one from GA-10 — so no query path can bypass it.

items.s: WHERE tenant_id = X on every query — enforce in code, test the enforcement
Isolation by construction; index sizes per tenant; no forgotten WHERE

scenes.narration: The three postures and their honesty levels. Filter-based scales best but lives one bug away from a breach — if you choose it, the enforcement lives in exactly one code path with tests that would fail a missing clause. Collections give structural isolation with modest overhead — the sweet spot for most SaaS tiers. And full separation for the clients whose contracts demand it — the cost is real and so is the assurance. The architect's move: make tenancy a provisioning decision per client tier, not a global one — and never, ever let a raw query bypass the retrieval interface.

scenes.title: Your index is **derived**. Your data is not.
scenes.sub: Back up the source; snapshot the index; rehearse the restore
scenes.narration: The disaster-recovery insight that simplifies everything: the vector index is a derived artifact. Given the source documents and the embedding model version, you can rebuild it. So the hierarchy of durability: source documents — irreplaceable, backed up like crown jewels; embeddings and metadata — derived, but expensive to regenerate — snapshot them; the index itself — fastest to rebuild, lowest backup priority. Your DR plan: R-P-O for the source data, a rebuild runbook with measured timings, and — the step everyone skips — a rehearsed restore. An untested backup is a rumor, not a plan.

items.s: Versioned, replicated, point-in-time recovery — the business asset
Store-level snapshots (Qdrant/pgbarman-style) cut restore from hours to minutes
Quarterly: rebuild the index from source in staging, measure time vs RTO

scenes.narration: The DR checklist, in priority order. Protect the source with the same rigor as any production database — because it is one. Snapshot the derived layers to meet aggressive R-T-Os — rebuilding a hundred-million-vector index might exceed your window, so snapshots buy back minutes you promised. And rehearse: schedule the restore drill, time it, compare against the R-T-O you wrote in the proposal. The difference between a recovery plan and a recovery fantasy is one afternoon of rehearsal per quarter. This is table stakes for any system holding client data.

scenes.title: Operations mastered — now the honest architecture talk
scenes.next: Reel 28 · Vector vs Parquet/SQL — when NOT to use vectors

recap: Deterministic IDs + upserts make re-ingestion idempotent; CDC beats rebuilds; deletes need budget
Size: N × dims × bytes × index overhead × 2 headroom; shard before the node fills; tenancy enforced in one code path
Source docs are the crown jewels; index is derived — snapshot for RTO, rehearse the restore

quiz.q: Re-ingesting a document after an edit creates duplicate chunks. What's the fix?
opts: Deterministic IDs (doc_id + chunk_index) so the same input replaces, never duplicates
quiz.why: Stable IDs make upserts idempotent by construction — re-running the pipeline converges instead of accumulating.

quiz.q: Which layer of a vector system deserves the strictest backup discipline?
opts: The source documents — irreplaceable; vectors and indexes are derived rebuildables
quiz.why: Index and embeddings are regenerable from source + model version; the source data is the true asset. Snapshots shorten restores, but source durability is non-negotiable.

opts: A missing tenant filter in any query path leaks data — enforcement must be structural and tested
quiz.why: Filter-based isolation is one forgotten WHERE clause from a breach — centralize enforcement in the retrieval interface and test that a bypass fails.

code.title: The operations layer — writes, tenancy, restore drill
code.body:
from hashlib import sha1

# --- 1. Deterministic upserts --------------------------------------
def chunk_id(doc_id: str, idx: int) -> str:
    return sha1(f"{doc_id}:{idx}".encode()).hexdigest()[:16]

for doc in changed_docs():              # from CDC events, not a rebuild
    for i, chunk in enumerate(chunk(doc.text)):
        store.upsert(id=chunk_id(doc.id, i),
                     vec=embed(chunk),
                     payload={"doc_id": doc.id, "v": doc.version,
                              "tenant": doc.tenant, "text": chunk})

# --- 2. Tenant enforcement (one path, tested) ----------------------
def search(q, tenant: str, k=5):
    assert tenant, "tenant is mandatory"
    return store.search(embed(q), k=k, where={"tenant": tenant})

# test:  search(q, tenant=None) must raise — CI enforces it

# --- 3. Restore drill (quarterly, timed) ---------------------------
def restore_drill():
    t0 = time.time()
    for doc in source_store.list_all():          # the crown jewels
        reindex(doc)                              # embed + upsert
    elapsed = time.time() - t0
    assert elapsed < RTO_SECONDS, f"rebuild {elapsed:.0f}s > RTO"
    # Snapshot alternative: store.snapshot() → restore in minutes

# --- 4. Delete = tombstone + compact -------------------------------
# store.delete(ids) marks; a scheduled job runs store.compact()
# off-peak — latency stays smooth, graph gets repaired.
annot: chunk_id is stable across re-runs — the idempotency trick
payload carries doc version: superseded chunks are replaceable on sight
The restore drill is a scheduled job, not a wiki page

notes:
# Operations

## Indexing & updates
- **Upsert** by deterministic ID (`sha1(doc_id:chunk_idx)`) → idempotent re-ingestion.
- Deletes: ANN graph repair is costly → tombstone + scheduled compact.
- **CDC** (source events) over periodic rebuilds; full rebuild = fallback.

## Sizing & cost
- Memory = N × dims × bytes × (1 + HNSW ~0.3-0.5) × 2 (headroom).
- Quantization (float16 / PQ) when memory bites — gate on golden-set recall.
- Plan sharding before the node fills; resharding full stores is surgery.

## Multi-tenancy & security
- Filter-based: cheap, one forgotten WHERE from a breach → enforce centrally + test.
- Per-tenant collections: structural isolation, moderate overhead — most SaaS tiers.
- Per-tenant DB/cluster: regulated tiers, cost follows assurance.

## Backup & DR
- **Source docs = crown jewels** (PIT recovery). Embeddings/index = derived → snapshots for RTO.
- Rehearse restores quarterly, time them against the promised RTO.
- Untested backup = rumor.
